stories.headline: Each AFL finalist's biggest September X factor
stories.summary: Footy finals are often decided in moments, so who are the 'moments men' for each AFL team featuring in September? Not many players are capable of being that man for their respective sides, but we think these guys could just be that difference.
stories.body:
Footy finals are often decided in moments, so who are the 'moments men' for each AFL team featuring in September?

Adelaide: Izak Rankine
Is there a player in the competition with a bigger point to prove this September than Rankine? The dynamic Crow famously missed out on last year's finals campaign after copping a four-game suspension for an anti-gay slur. Rankine is already the ultimate X factor, but given he'll feel as if he owes his side after that 2025 indiscretion, we might just be set to watch him reach another level. And that's saying something! No player has been more productive than Rankine over the past eight weeks. His last appearance was particularly memorable, tallying 35 disposals and booting four goals in a win over GWS.

Brisbane: Zac Bailey

This could be the last finals series in which we see Bailey wearing maroon, blue, and gold. The 26-year-old restricted free agent is one of the most in-demand players this offseason, with offers from the Lions and Crows reportedly nearing up to $10 million over seven years. But enough about the off-field, it's his play on the field which is the focus here. Bailey has the ability to rip games to shreds quickly; a multiple goal kicker in 10 games this year, he's averaging career-highs in Rating Points, disposals, metres gained, and clearances. Bailey's become a complete player at the Lions, and with other star names like Lachie Neale, Will Ashcroft, and Hugh McCluggage perhaps taking the attention, he could be in for a big finals series.

Carlton: Jagga Smith
If Smith's first final was any indication of the type of big-game player he is, then Carlton fans will be salivating at the prospect of him wearing the navy blue jumper for the next decade. Smith torched the Demons on Saturday night, finishing with 29 disposals and two goals, lifting his side into an elimination final. The 2026 AFL Rising Star has poise, an elite work rate, great skills, and a mature head, traits that hold you in good stead come September. With so much attention rightly on midfield teammates Patrick Cripps and Sam Walsh, don't be surprised if Smith flies under the radar and proves the difference during this finals series.

Fremantle: Shai Bolton
Would it surprise you to learn Bolton hasn't booted more than two goals in a single game this year? Perhaps you can point to the team success and spread of contributions as a reason, or his increased minutes up the ground (he's attended a career-high 60% of centre bounces), but his 21 goals is the lowest return in a season since 2020 (the COVID year). All that really means is there's another gear for Bolton to engage, and he has a detailed history of hitting the scoreboard and doing significant damage in big moments. Watch out for Shai this finals series.

Geelong: Ollie Dempsey
The 2026 All-Australian wing looms as a difference-maker in this finals series. After a career-best home-and-away year in which he booted 30 goals, Dempsey has form in performing in September. He kicked three goals in the qualifying final last year against the Lions, and then four goals in the losing Grand Final (also against the Lions). His ability to hold width, run all day, get back to defend, and then stretch forward to pop up in the goal square is unmatched across the league. And after a long year, there may be some tired bodies lining up against him. He'll outrun them all.

Hawthorn: Nick Watson
It might seem obvious but could it really be anyone else? The Wizard has well and truly lived up to his nickname in 2026, establishing himself as the competition's premier small forward and earning much deserved All-Australian selection last month. The energetic Hawk has booted a ridiculous 55 goals this season and threatens to hit the scoreboard just about every time the Sherrin is in his vicinity. Watson has already featured in five finals in his young career and has kicked goals in all of them. At this point we just expect him to rise to the big game occasion.

Sydney: Charlie Curnow
You might be thinking 'Curnow, an X factor ... huh?!' Stick with us. Whether fair or not, Curnow has developed a little bit of a reputation of being a finals flopper. In his time at the Blues he featured in three finals and managed just a single goal in each of those games. Those three finals all came in 2023, the same year he won the Coleman Medal with 78 majors. Curnow will be desperate to change the narrative and the Swans will need him to more than ever given last month's controversy and the depleted team that will take to the field this September.

Western Bulldogs: Arty Jones
Okay, we're jumping on the bandwagon as it's already rolling, but Jones is in fine form, and could be the guy to be the difference in another final for the Bulldogs. In general, key forwards kick fewer goals in finals, while small and general forwards do more damage, and after his career-best return of four majors against the Magpies in their wildcard clash, we're backing Arty to have even more impact in September. Two of his highest-rated games ever have come in the past fortnight (vs. Melbourne in Round 24 and vs. Collingwood in the wildcard) -- can he keep it going?

stories.headline: What makes Max Verstappen so good? Career, background and F1 records
stories.summary: Max Verstappen is returning to his racing roots and is facing 100 drivers in a unique event called Max vs. 100 where the Formula 1 star will attempt to overtake 100 challengers, starting from the back of the grid.
stories.body:
Max Verstappen is returning to his racing roots and is taking part in a unique event called Max vs 100 where the Formula 1 star will attempt to overtake 100 drivers, starting from the back of the grid.

The 28-year-old currently races in F1, the highest tier in motorsport. He is one of the fiercest competitors out there and is known for his aggressive driving style and fearless overtaking.

But if you have never heard of him, or want to learn more, here is everything you need to know.

- Max vs 100: F1 superstar Verstappen to race drivers in karting event - live on Disney+

Who is Max Verstappen?
Verstappen was born in Belgium to his Dutch father Jos and his Belgian mother Sophie. His father raced in F1 between 1994-2003 and had two podium finishes, while his mother competed in karts. He currently resides in Monaco.

Who does he race for?
Verstappen started racing go-karts when he was just four years old and started to compete in championships at seven.

He then made his way through the ranks winning several world and European titles in 2013. He raced just one season in Formula 3 before skipping Formula 2 and heading straight to Formula 1.

In 2015, he signed for Red Bull junior team Toro Rosso at the age of 17 before he was promoted to Red Bull a year later.

He then went on to become the youngest ever grand prix winner after taking victory at the Spanish Grand Prix and has been at Red Bull ever since, becoming the most successful driver at the team.

He signed a long-term contract back in March 2022 to stay at the Milton Keynes-based team until the end of 2028, and before the Dutch Grand Prix this year he penned a new deal keeping him at the team until 2030.

What has he achieved?
It was clear from the early days that Verstappen was going to be an exceptional racing driver and he's become a phenomenon since with a killer instinct.

He's had 244 race starts in F1 and has been on the top step of the podium 71 times. He's been on the podium 131 times and is just two pole positions away from reaching 50 career poles.

The Dutchman has four world championships which he won back-to-back in a dominant Red Bull era between 2021-2024.

He also has an impressive list of achievements to his name, one being in 2023 where he recorded the most wins [19] and the most podium finishes [21] in a single season. He also recorded 10 consecutive race victories.

When is Max vs 100?
The event is taking place on Sept. 16 and will be streamed live on Disney+.

Why is he racing in Max vs 100?

Verstappen has never been shy of getting his teeth stuck into other forms of motorsport away from Formula 1. He most recently made his debut at the iconic Nürburgring 24 Hours in May, driving a Mercedes-AMG GT3.

This will be a slightly different challenge for the Dutchman, but no doubt one he will enjoy with his competitive nature.

"In go-karts you learn all the basics: starts, defending, overtaking," Verstappen said. "Of course, I spent a long period of my life go-karting, so it's always nice to return."

The event is taking place at Silverstone in the U.K. and a circuit has been purpose-built for the occasion. It's set to be the biggest go-kart event in the world.

- Max Verstappen deal: Good news for Red Bull and F1, bad news for the driver market

- Max Verstappen ends F1 speculation by signing new Red Bull contract to 2030

How is his 2026 F1 season going?
The 2026 season is one with big regulation and rules changes and Red Bull are currently at the back of the front running teams, but are ahead of the midfield pack.

Verstappen is still searching for his first race win of the season, but has been on the podium four times.

He's currently sixth in the title championship and is 130 points adrift from title leader Kimi Antonelli.

stories.headline: Song Yadong KO's Umar Nurmagomedov in massive UFC upset
stories.summary: Song Yadong pulled off a massive upset by knocking out heavily favored Umar Nurmagomedov in the men's bantamweight main event of UFC Fight Night in Shanghai.
stories.body:
Song Yadong saved the greatest performance of his career for his home country, knocking out former title challenger Umar Nurmagomedov in the men's bantamweight main event of UFC Fight Night on Saturday in Shanghai.

Song (24-9-1, 1 NC), a nearly 5-1 underdog at DraftKings Sportsbook, dropped Nurmagomedov with a short right hand, drawing a roar from the crowd when the fight was waved off at 1 minute, 48 seconds of Round 2.

"I believe in myself, and my team believed that I would win this fight," Song said through an interpreter. "They told me I would knock this guy out, and I did it."

It was the second straight fight in China for Song and his second straight win by finish. His most recent knockout win had been in 2023.

Song, making his first appearance in Shanghai since his UFC debut at age 19 in 2017, walked out to a hero's welcome.

"Nine years ago, I wanted to show I could walk in this Octagon," he said. "Nine years later, I want to prove I am the best in the world. I am the best Chinese fighter in the world."

The knockout came after Nurmagomedov (20-2) ducked out of the way of a left hand and right into the path of a short right hand, which connected near his right ear and sent him limply to the canvas. Song delivered three finishing shots on the mat before the referee jumped in.

That sent Song running around inside the cage in celebration, where he nearly ran into Nurmagomedov's younger brother and cornerman, PFL lightweight champion Usman Nurmagomedov, who had rushed in to check on his fallen brother. Usman Nurmagomedov appeared to throw an elbow in Song's direction as the elated winner was running past.

Song climbed atop the cage to soak in the fans' cheers before jumping down outside the cage and running into the crowd to get hugs and high-fives from fans.

"Maybe not today, maybe not tomorrow, maybe not next month, but I will be the first male Chinese UFC champion," Song said through the interpreter, with the "male" designation a nod to countrywoman Zhang Weili, a two-time women's champion at strawweight.

Song, who trains in Sacramento, California, switched to English and yelled, "Give me the title shot!"

stories.headline: Jets star goalie Connor Hellebuyck confirms trade request
stories.summary: Three-time Vezina Trophy-winning goaltender Connor Hellebuyck publicly confirmed Thursday that he asked the Winnipeg Jets to trade him.
stories.body:
WINNIPEG, Manitoba -- Three-time Vezina Trophy-winning goaltender Connor Hellebuyck publicly confirmed Thursday that he asked the Winnipeg Jets to trade him.

In a statement released by his agent, Ray Petkau, Hellebuyck said he made the request several months ago and "tried to handle the situation quietly and respectfully while giving the organization time to explore its options."

Hellebuyck said he felt it was important to go public because training camp is fast approaching. Camps are set to open in roughly three weeks.

"My position has not changed, and I believe moving on is the best path forward for me and my family," Hellebuyck said. "(I) hope a resolution can be reached soon."

Hellebuyck, 33, has played his entire NHL career with the Jets and was voted MVP in the 2024-25 season. He backstopped the U.S. to the gold medal at the Olympics in February.

A team spokesperson did not immediately respond to a message seeking comment.

Trade rumors swirled about Hellebuyck in late June around the draft, but nothing came to fruition. The Michigan native missed time because of injury and had a career-worst .895 save percentage last season as Winnipeg underachieved expectations and missed the playoffs.

But his track record and body of work are among the best at the position over the past decade. His 345 wins, 2.58 goals-against average and .916 save percentage since entering the league in 2015 are second only to Tampa Bay two-time Stanley Cup champion Andrei Vasilevskiy.

Hellebuyck has not enjoyed the same postseason success as Vasilevskiy and the Lightning. He's 24-34, with the Jets only making it past the second round and into the Western Conference final once, back in 2018.

He signed an eight-year, $59.5 million extension with Winnipeg in October 2023. He's under contract through 2031 at a salary cap hit of $8.5 million.

"Winnipeg has been my home for my entire NHL career, and I will always be grateful for my time there," Hellebuyck said. "I appreciate everything Winnipeg Jets fans have meant to me throughout my career."

stories.headline: NRL Midweek Mail R27: Tigers winger garnering rival interest
stories.summary: Blake Lawrie will earn a rare start this weekend before he heads off to join the Super League, while the future of his Dragons teammate Tyrell Sloan is still a little uncertain.
stories.body:
The NRL rarely stands still.

Between training sessions, media appearances, and behind-the-scenes conversations, new storylines often begin to emerge before the weekend arrives.

Throughout the week, ESPN will be gathering notes, insights, and updates from around the competition heading into Round 27 of the NRL.

Bears eye Dragons hooker

The Perth Bears have expressed interest in signing St George Illawarra hooker Connor Muhleisen as they continue to build their inaugural NRL roster.

Muhleisen is off-contract at the end of the season and has emerged as an option for the Bears, who are continuing to scour the market for players ahead of their 2027 entry into the competition.

ESPN understands Perth have shown interest in the 25-year-old, although the Dragons have also indicated they are open to retaining the local junior beyond this season.

Muhleisen has spent his entire career in the Dragons system and made his NRL debut for the club in 2023.

Skelton form sparks rival interest

Off-contract Wests Tigers winger Jeral Skelton is beginning to attract interest from rival clubs after an impressive finish to the season.

Skelton has produced some of his best football over the past fortnight, crossing for three tries across his past two appearances while providing the Tigers with plenty of punch coming out of their own end.

The powerful outside back carried the ball 20 times for 152 metres in the Tigers' clash with the Roosters, backing up a 130-metre performance against North Queensland.

ESPN understands Skelton's recent form has begun to generate interest around the NRL as clubs assess their outside-back options for next season.

Lawrie lands new club

170-game Dragons veteran Blake Lawrie has landed his next destination, with sources informing ESPN that he's agreed to a three-year deal with the York Knights in the Super League.

After it was announced by St George Illawarra that he'd be departing the club at the end of the 2026 season, ESPN can reveal he is bound for England.

He had garnered interest from the Catalans Dragons, before opting to sign with the Knights.

Lawrie will be named in the No. 10 jumper for the Red V in his final game as a Dragon this weekend.

Sloan's future may yet be in red and white

Doubt has clouded Tyrell Sloan's move to the Castleford Tigers in 2027, and while he says he "still signed a contract" and intends to honour it at his next club, the prospect of returning to the Dragons remains a possibility to him.

"Honestly, my manager works hard, and he's really good at his job," he said when asked if there's any conversations around a potential backflip to remain at the Red V.

"Whatever happens, it's going to be for the best reason and again, I've signed a contract, so I do want to make that clear."

He went on to say he hopes that this weekend won't be his last as a Dragon.

stories.headline: Facts vs. Feelings: In on Ladd McConkey? Out on Bucky Irving? What about Lamar Jackson?
stories.summary: In advance of the biggest draft weekend, Liz Loza reveals her strongest thoughts to help you have a successful draft.
stories.body:
Pithy quotes written in hot pink script. Video footage from late-night talk shows. Audio clips of live(ly) performances. The internet has attempted to celebrate Dolly Parton's memory with the volume and breadth befitting an icon.

Except there can never be enough for a person whose most adored trait was being too much. A living, breathing anomaly. Humble yet confident. Ambitious but kind. Petite and powerful. What made Dolly unique wasn't just that she did everything on her own terms and in her own way ... but that her unapologetic approach actually worked.

From shading Elvis to building an amusement park in the Smoky Mountains, Dolly's principles guided her business acumen. It's almost as if her conviction carried her career ... not the other way around.

Often in life, we spend so much time worrying about making the "right" decision that we forget why we're making it in the first place. For the intended result or for the enjoyment of the process? Ideally, both. Sometimes, the factors are so complex that decisions can't simply be influenced by fact. We gotta get into some feels.

We also have to acknowledge that we might whiff. Decision-making isn't a science. The algorithms and chatbots would like us to believe differently, suggesting (demanding?) that perfection is possible and efficiency is essential.

What they're missing is actual lived experience. A cellular understanding that the vector between choice and resolution does not, in fact, exist in a straight line. It's all swirly. Full of zigzags and beautifully jagged edges. Those spikes and slopes aren't just the data accrued but, also, lessons learned. Like Ms. Dolly said, "If you want the rainbow, you gotta put up with the rain."

Surrendering to fallibility makes room for ease. Viewing mistakes as opportunities -- rather than dead ends -- alters the trajectory of enjoyment. And all this relates to fantasy football.

For example, I could be totally wrong about Christian McCaffrey this year. Maybe he'll be the first running back in two decades to come off a 450-touch season (including the playoffs) and finish inside the top 10 fantasy producers at the position. The tomes of research I've uncovered suggest otherwise. That evidence hasn't stopped folks from screaming at the wind (and me). But my commitment to the facts in combination with my personal conviction keeps me from bending the knee.

It also keeps me smiling. Because there's satisfaction in standing 10 toes down when you've done the work. My fantasy team doesn't belong to the consensus. Yours shouldn't either. So draft with the confidence your squad deserves. Whether that's leaning into Christian Watson's volatility or eschewing Jakobi Meyers' floor, make this a signature season. And remember one more bit of wisdom from Dolly: "If you keep yourself out of the game for fear of losing, there is no way on this earth you're gonna win."

With that in mind, let's dig in for a closer look at the facts -- and feelings -- surrounding some of the biggest names in fantasy football this season.

Lamar Jackson, QB, Baltimore Ravens
Coming off career-low rushing numbers, Jackson's redraft stock has plummeted. A deeper dive into the numbers reveals massive bounce-back appeal at an all-time discount. Jackson battled hamstring, toe, ankle and back injuries throughout the past season, missing four contests and playing through the pain for a handful of others. Before suffering the initial injury in Week 4, Jackson averaged 27.6 FPPG and was on pace for 30 passing scores. Even in a down effort, the Ravens QB averaged 18.1 FPPG in the games he was able to finish.

Jackson enters 2026 fully healthy and primed for a rebound. Backed by the NFL's fifth-easiest strength of schedule, Jackson's aerial appeal skyrockets with the addition of a rookie pass-catching quartet: wideouts Ja'Kobi Lane and Elijah Sarratt, alongside tight ends Matthew Hibner and Josh Cuevas. This influx of young talent meshes perfectly with new offensive coordinator Declan Doyle's aggressive, big-play philosophy. A conservative projection of just 120 rushing attempts still easily clears his path back to a top-five fantasy finish. Given the two-round gap between Josh Allen and Jackson, the Ravens QB is a strong value at his current ADP of right around 35.

James Cook III, RB, Buffalo Bills
It wasn't Derrick Henry or Jonathan Taylor or Bijan Robinson who led the NFL in rushing yards last season. It was Cook. Amassing a career-high 1,612 rushing yards, Cook remained one of the slipperiest backs in the league, closing out the year as fantasy's RB5 in breakaway runs (16) and the RB7 in evaded tackles (77). Buoyed by an elite offensive line, the 26-year-old additionally managed 3.09 yards before contact (RB3, behind Jahmyr Gibbs and Blake Corum).

Ranking fourth at the position in scrimmage yards, Cook's ground numbers weren't the only stats to surge. The dual-threat talent also added 4.4 FPPG via receiving work. That's particularly noteworthy given new offensive coordinator Pete Carmichael's comments about getting Cook more involved in the passing game. Carmichael previously served as the New Orleans Saints' offensive coordinator when New Orleans selected Alvin Kamara in the third round of the 2017 NFL draft. Given Cook's projected volume, upside as a receiver and consistent weekly floor (only six games outside of the top 10 at the position in 2025), the Bills' RB1 is worthy of a first-round virtual selection.

Bucky Irving, RB, Tampa Bay Buccaneers
Undersized but ultra-aggressive, Irving tore up the back half of his rookie campaign, becoming a premier fantasy asset in the process. Unfortunately, his high-impact approach took a physical toll, causing injuries that derailed the bulk of his second season. The Oregon product missed seven games due to a midfoot sprain and simultaneous shoulder dislocation suffered in Week 4 of 2025. The shoulder issue ultimately required offseason surgery, causing a recovery process that stretched into 2026. Even though Irving did not miss any preseason action specifically due to the shoulder, there remains hesitation about his ability to handle a robust workload.

Enter Kenny Gainwell. Tampa Bay let Rachaad White walk and replaced him with Gainwell, who is fresh off a career season in Pittsburgh. The RB4 in catches (73) and the RB5 in receiving yards (486), Gainwell posted the highest percentage of fantasy points via receptions (62%) in 2025. Given that 53% (RB5) of Irving's fantasy points were earned through the air and just 47% of his virtual production came from the rush, Irving's totals figure to recede. Factor in Sean Tucker's propensity for goal-line touchdown poaching and Bucky's 2026 profile appears increasingly bleak.

Ladd McConkey, WR, Los Angeles Chargers
Who will be this year's JSN? It's a question I've been frequently asked over the spring and summer. While each season unfolds as its own unique expression and, therefore, such signature breakouts can't be guaranteed, identifying overlapping situations and players can be a useful exercise.

Much like Smith-Njigba, McConkey enters his third season boasting positional versatility and a history of being heavily targeted (over 100 looks in back-to-back efforts). While McConkey has done significant damage from the slot, his capacity to win across the formation aligns well with the arrival of new offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel. Just as Klint Kubiak expanded Smith-Njigba's route tree, McDaniel is primed to unlock a new tier of deployment for McConkey.

Anchored by Justin Herbert's deft arm talent and elevated by a swath of available targets -- inheriting the opportunities left behind by Keenan Allen, similar to the way JSN absorbed a void left by DK Metcalf -- McConkey stands at the precipice of a career-defining season. His underlying metrics prove he has the profile to capitalize on this workload, flashing exceptional efficiency and playmaking upside by averaging a stellar 2.79 yards per route run as a rookie. When stacked against the less-than-inspiring veteran wideouts typically available in the fifth round, McConkey's ceiling calls like a siren's song.

Mike Evans, WR, San Francisco 49ers
Already skipping reps, Evans is a dicey proposition entering his age-33 season. Hamstring and collarbone issues sidelined the vet for nine games in 2025. A change of scenery does not appear to have provided relief, as he has battled calf, quad and groin injuries thus far into training camp. Even when he does suit up, the physical wear and tear on his body appears to have caught up with his production. Evans posted career lows in yards per route run (a 33.3% drop from 2024) and fantasy points per catch last season. The dip in efficiency capped the impact of his previously high-value grabs.

On the other hand, the red area of the field is exactly where Evans has thrived, ranking third of 77 qualified WRs in percentage of points scored via TD (38.8%) over the past three seasons. Combined with learning a new playbook and facing a bottom-10 strength of schedule, Evans faces an uphill battle to rebound in 2026.

Rashid Shaheed, WR, Seattle Seahawks
Seattle re-signed Shaheed to a three-year, $51 million contract, signaling an increased role in the offense. The 27-year-old's previous experience in New Orleans indicates that he's up for the task. Shaheed averaged 11.6 FPPG alongside Chris Olave prior to being traded midseason. He also registered an impressive 22% target share (not much lower than Olave's 29% target share) from Weeks 1 through 9. Furthermore, Shaheed's 7.3 targets and 4.9 receptions per contest ranked 15th among wide receivers during that span.

Reports out of training camp suggest that the Seahawks plan to use Shaheed in the short-to-intermediate passing game, lifting the speedster's weekly floor above his usual deep-threat status. Because all other Seattle wide receivers -- outside of Smith-Njigba -- combined for a mere 82 catches, 1,100 yards and eight touchdowns last season, Shaheed has a massive opportunity to absorb that production and lock himself in as the team's clear-cut No. 2 WR. He is an absolute bull's-eye of a late-round dart throw in upcoming fantasy drafts.

Colston Loveland, TE, Chicago Bears
No need to waste your energy debating between Rome Odunze and Luther Burden III for Bears pass catchers -- Loveland is the guy to roster. Equal parts reliable and dynamic, the No. 10 pick from a year ago figures draw a significant number of the 150 looks vacated due to the departures of Olamide Zaccheaus (65) and D.J. Moore (85). A sudden mover for his size (6-foot-6, 248 pounds), Loveland wins at the catch point and remains a threat after the catch. He averaged an impressive 1.96 yards per route run (TE6) as a 21-year-old rookie.

Unleashed by Ben Johnson down the stretch, the Michigan standout emerged as fantasy TE2 (behind only Trey McBride) from Weeks 9 through 18 of last year. He averaged a heart-stopping 12.0 targets, 7.0 catches and 94.5 receiving yards over his final four games (including the playoffs). There's little reason to believe he won't pick up where he left off. A staggering mismatch over the middle of the field, Loveland has TE1 appeal. He's a prime target at the position in the fourth round of fantasy drafts.
